extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, referees, and researchers interested in mathematical peer review and proof verification
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and standards for refereeing mathematics papers: what referees are expected to check about correctness, how they check it in practice, and how editors use reports to judge papers. Includes community/post-publication validation and editorial decision trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary responsibility for correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is 100% the responsibility of the author but it is also 85% the responsibility of the referee.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and interviewees locate primary accountability with the author — authors must vouch for their results. Referees have an accountability role but are not expected to carry full burden for correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee must be reasonably convinced / plausibility check
rubrics_metrics.description: Official guideline: ‘the referee must be reasonably convinced of the accuracy of the paper’ (AMS, 2015). Editors want referees ‘to convince themselves it’s most likely to be true’ and be ‘pretty confident that is really right’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice referees perform a ‘plausibility check’—hoping to catch mistakes but not guaranteeing absolute certainty. Reports often state varying degrees of confidence (e.g., ‘I could follow the argument in detail and did not find any mistakes’ vs ‘The proof is correct I think’).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal vs practical extent of checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally checking every line, but in practice referees rely on experience and heuristics: ‘in practice I think there’s going to be a lot of, “okay I understand what technique they’re applying… and I know from experience that this is a standard thing that’s going to work.”’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize gap between ideals and feasible workload: while the ideal is line-by-line verification, practical refereeing uses expert judgement to check plausibility and key steps rather than every detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectively checking the paper’s skeleton and key arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees typically ‘look for the skeleton of the paper, identify the steps that I thought … and then … work down trying to fill in the argument.’ They find ‘turning points’ or ‘key arguments’ to read in greater detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with an overview of structure, identify bottlenecks/turning points, focus effort on those key places rather than exhaustive line-by-line checks. Use subject expertise to locate likely problem spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skimming plausible parts / focusing on suspicious parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees ‘skip over the elements they deem plausible or reasonable’ and read parts that look ‘suspicious’ or ‘unlikely’ in much greater detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristics: accept familiar standard techniques with less scrutiny; scrutinize places that 'seem a bit too strong', where methods look too weak, or where writing/detail level changes. Beware that mistakes may hide in plausible-looking regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on referee expertise and familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: One part of referee expertise is being familiar enough with the subject to quickly identify where key places are: ‘[referees] know what can go wrong.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign referees with real expertise in the paper's methods/topic; referees' prior work in the area allows them to identify bottlenecks and likely failure modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in effort between reports; editorial remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: There is huge variety in the amount of work referees put in; some reports are ‘too sketchy’ or cover only part of the paper. Editors sometimes ask for a second report or, reluctantly, accept on basis of an unsatisfactory report because of delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should assess report thoroughness; consider soliciting additional reviews when confidence is low, but balance with time pressures and backlog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of journal standing on scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The higher the standing of the journal, the more the editors feel that the work of the referee has to be technically correct.’ Conversely, lower-level journals may have less rigorous refereeing (though paradoxically sometimes better because reviewers have more time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect more careful technical checking for top journals and for manuscripts judged of high importance or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author reputation influences checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees may check known authors less carefully than unknown ones; reputation is taken into account but only within certain subject areas: ‘we only trust authors in certain areas’ and may check more carefully if an author writes outside their normal field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use author reputation as one factor in assessing necessary scrutiny, but beware pitfalls: reputational trust can miss subtle deep errors; negative reputations (sloppy authors) can also influence referee selection and caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-blind vs double-blind considerations and bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing in mathematics is typically single-blind. Double-blind aims to battle bias and ‘supports inclusivity and diversity’ (AMS, 2022). In single-blind refereeing, referees may not check proofs of known authors as carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize bias risks in single-blind systems; double-anonymity can reduce implicit bias but may be impractical in some math subfields due to preprints and specialized communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing types of referee-detected problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems range from trivial typos to serious mistakes that ‘kill the result’. The most common substantive issue referees report is insufficient detail or a ‘gap’ in a proof rather than an outright error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify issues in reports (typos, minor fixes, gaps, fundamental errors) and request appropriate remedies: errata, additional detail, revision, or rejection/withdrawal for fatal flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling gaps: request more detail / assess fixability
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaps are places where authors left too much to the reader; referees often ask authors to provide more details. Sometimes the author can fill the gap; sometimes filling one gap causes changes elsewhere; sometimes the gap is irreparable and leads to withdrawal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors for clarifying details and proofs for problematic steps; assess whether fixes are local and feasible. If iterations fail, consider rejecting or requesting withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals that trigger detailed scrutiny (red flags)
rubrics_metrics.description: Red flags include results that ‘seem a bit too strong’, methods that seem too weak for claimed results, sudden changes in level of detail, lackadaisical write-up, or parts that do not fit with known literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such signals appear, read those portions line-by-line, request detailed justifications, and possibly seek specialist reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of referee patience / diminishing returns in revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees may become unwilling to continue after multiple troubled revisions: ‘If the next revision has similar problems … this will be my last round with this paper.’ Editors may adopt a ‘three strikes and the author’s out’ policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set expectations about number of revision cycles; consider transfer or rejection when referee/time investment is exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication and iterative resolution (referee-author dialogue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee-author exchanges (e.g., Wiles and Katz) can resolve suspected gaps; some problems can be answered by correspondence, converting apparent gaps into resolved arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct queries and iterative correspondence to resolve unclear steps when feasible before escalating to rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement on citing accepted work / not relying on unpublished results
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may require that if a paper relies on a result, that result must be at least accepted for publication somewhere: ‘If the paper relies on something that’s not at least accepted for publication somewhere, then we say, “no”.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid building essential claims on unpublished or non-accepted sources; editors should enforce policy on reliance on published/accepted literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication community scrutiny and time requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainty about a result increases with time and use: prizes may require ‘at least two years must have passed since publication’ and ‘the proposed solution must have received general acceptance in the global mathematics community’ (Clay Mathematics Institute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize peer review as necessary but not sufficient; community validation and integrative usage of results over time are central to establishing long-term correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review’s additional roles beyond correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review ‘adds a bit of certainty’ and contributes substantially to improved presentation; it ensures that a paper is read carefully by at least one person and helps judge importance as well as correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate submissions not only for technical correctness but also clarity, exposition, and significance; use peer review to improve presentation and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty is probabilistic; published ≠ guaranteed correct
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Being published in a journal is not a certificate for correctness’ and ‘if it goes through the peer review process, that’s not a guarantee that absolutely everything is correct, but it means it’s pretty plausible.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat publication as raising plausibility rather than delivering certainty; encourage readers and subsequent researchers to perform integrative checks when using results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community responsibility and specialist subfield knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The expertise necessary to evaluate a paper ‘resides in the mathematical community’ and different specialist subfields may judge claims differently; community interaction over years functions as a ‘sieve’ filtering errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should seek referees with relevant subfield expertise; understand that some proofs require broader community engagement before consensus is reached, and that acceptance may vary across subcommunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial trade-offs under resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors face trade-offs from ‘too many papers, not enough referees’ and may reluctantly accept imperfect reports to avoid further delay; the system is ‘under stress’ though not necessarily collapsed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about resource constraints, consider policies to manage referee load (e.g., selective checking, limiting rounds), and use additional safeguards (extra reviewers, editorial checks) for high-impact or suspicious papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report language and inference by editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees use varying formulations of confidence (from definitive certification to hedged statements). Editors interpret these as signals of effort and confidence: detailed reports increase editorial confidence; sketchy reports may prompt second opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should state level of checking performed explicitly (e.g., what was checked in detail vs skimmed). Editors should calibrate decisions based on report thoroughness and phrasing.
